raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an established nonpharmacological strategy for stroke prevention in selected patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF). Its rationale rests on the observation that most thrombi in non-valvular AF arise in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated embryologic remnant whose contractile dysfunction during AF promotes stasis, endothelial dysfunction and thrombogenesis [1,2]. LAA anatomy is highly variable; ostial size, depth, lobar complexity and morphology influence both embolic risk and device selection [3].

Oral anticoagulation remains the default stroke-prevention therapy for most eligible patients with AF. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have improved safety and convenience compared with warfarin in pivotal trials [4-6]. Nevertheless, anticoagulation may be unsuitable because of prior intracranial or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding, extreme frailty, drug interactions, nonadherence, advanced renal dysfunction, or occupational bleeding risk. LAAC therefore aims to uncouple stroke prevention from chronic systemic anticoagulation, accepting an upfront procedural risk in exchange for durable mechanical exclusion of the LAA.

The field began with endocardial occlusion using the PLAATO system, demonstrating procedural feasibility in high-risk AF cohorts [7,8]. The Watchman device subsequently became the best-studied platform. In PROTECT AF, Watchman was non-inferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism and cardiovascular death, although early procedural complications were more frequent [9]. Operator experience and device iteration reduced complications, as shown in subsequent analyses and registries [10]. Residual peri-device leak was common but usually small; its clinical significance remains nuanced, with larger leaks generally prompting closer surveillance [11]. Longer follow-up from PROTECT AF, PREVAIL and pooled analyses suggested comparable ischemic stroke prevention, fewer hemorrhagic strokes, and potential reductions in cardiovascular and all-cause mortality compared with warfarin [12-15].

Evidence in patients unable to take warfarin has come mainly from nonrandomized studies. The ASAP study supported Watchman implantation followed by dual antiplatelet therapy rather than warfarin in patients with contraindications to oral anticoagulation [16]. EWOLUTION broadened real-world experience, including many patients at high bleeding risk, and reported high implant success with acceptable early and 1-year outcomes [17,18]. The United States NCDR LAAO Registry confirmed that contemporary practice achieves high procedural success, although pericardial effusion, major bleeding, vascular complications and device embolization remain important hazards [19]. The newer Watchman FLX improved conformability, sealing and recapturability, with favorable short-term safety and closure performance in PINNACLE FLX [20].

Alternative endocardial devices include the Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and Amulet. Early European and Canadian experiences showed feasibility in patients often unsuitable for anticoagulation [21,22]. In the randomized Amulet IDE trial, Amulet achieved non-inferior safety and effectiveness compared with Watchman, with more complete LAA sealing but somewhat different procedural complication profiles [23]. Thus, device choice is increasingly anatomy- and operator-dependent rather than dictated by a single evidence base.

Randomized comparison with DOACs is particularly relevant in contemporary AF care. PRAGUE-17 enrolled high-risk patients and found LAAC non-inferior to DOAC therapy for a composite of ischemic and bleeding outcomes [24]. Four-year follow-up supported sustained non-inferiority, with reductions in nonprocedural bleeding emerging over time [25]. These data are important but not definitive: sample sizes remain modest, event rates are low, and results apply to carefully selected high-risk patients treated in experienced centers.

Epicardial LAA exclusion with the LARIAT suture system offers a different concept: ligation rather than implantation of a permanent endocardial plug. Initial and multicenter experiences showed feasibility but raised concerns regarding pericardial access complications, inflammatory effusions and incomplete closure [26,27]. Consequently, endocardial occluders dominate current practice.

Successful LAAC depends on careful patient selection, imaging and post-procedural antithrombotic management. Pre-procedural transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac computed tomography excludes LAA thrombus and defines anatomy; intraprocedural transesophageal or intracardiac echocardiography guides transseptal puncture, sizing, deployment stability and leak assessment. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in a minority of patients but is clinically relevant because it is associated with stroke and systemic embolism [28]. Post-implant regimens vary: the original Watchman trials used warfarin plus aspirin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy, whereas contemporary practice frequently uses DOAC-based, dual-antiplatelet, or single-antiplatelet strategies tailored to bleeding risk [29]. Consensus documents emphasize multidisciplinary evaluation, shared decision-making and follow-up imaging to detect DRT or significant leak [30].

In summary, percutaneous LAAC has matured from a niche intervention to a guideline-supported option for AF patients with compelling reasons to avoid long-term anticoagulation. Its strongest role is not as a universal substitute for DOACs, but as individualized therapy for patients in whom bleeding risk, intolerance or adherence challenges erode the net benefit of anticoagulation. Future priorities include larger DOAC-era randomized trials, better prediction of DRT and leak-related risk, simplified antithrombotic regimens, and comparative effectiveness studies across devices and imaging strategies.
